title: Alert on symptoms, not noise
summary: Compute availability from request data, review noisy alert rules, and reason about SLOs and error budgets.

scenario.briefing: The on-call rotation gets paged for CPU above forty percent, but nobody pages when checkout latency doubles. The dashboard reports request counts, not availability, and the alert file has grown one rule per incident. Start by computing availability from the request log.

objectives.description: Compute availability and error counts per service.
Identify noisy and missing alert conditions.
Explain symptoms, SLOs, burn rate, and cardinality.

hints: Availability is successful requests divided by all requests.
Treat 5xx responses as errors; 4xx responses are usually client errors.
Group by service and round consistently.
Alert on user-visible symptoms such as error rate and latency, not raw CPU alone.

misconceptions.description: Reporting request counts without a success ratio.
misconceptions.feedback: Counts do not show whether users succeeded. Divide successful requests by total requests for each service.
A single error can be noise. Alert on sustained error-budget burn or a user-visible symptom with a duration window.
Alert fatigue hides real incidents. Every page should be actionable and tied to a symptom users feel.

sections.title: Measure what users experience
sections.body: Availability is the share of requests that succeed. Latency is how long they take. A dashboard full of CPU and memory can miss a checkout path that is failing while the machines look healthy.

sections.title: Page on symptoms with a window
sections.body: A page should wake someone for a sustained, user-visible problem. A single 5xx is not a page; a burn rate that would exhaust the error budget within hours is. Use a duration window to suppress spikes.

sections.title: Every alert needs an action
sections.body: If the responder cannot do anything differently after the page, it is a dashboard signal, not an alert. High cardinality labels such as user id multiply series and cost; keep labels bounded.

steps.title: Compute availability per service
steps.prompt: Edit availability.sql. Return service, total request count, error count, and availability rounded to three decimals for each service, ordered by service. Treat status 500 and above as an error.
hints: Group the request rows by service.
Count all rows and count the rows with status at least 500.
Divide successful rows by all rows as a decimal.
Use CASE inside SUM for both counts and round the ratio.

files.content:
SELECT service,
       COUNT(*) AS total,
       0 AS errors,
       1.0 AS availability
FROM requests
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY service;

database.schemaSql: CREATE TABLE requests (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, service TEXT NOT NULL, status INTEGER NOT NULL, latency_ms INTEGER NOT NULL, ts TEXT NOT NULL);

steps.title: Review the alert rules
steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.
hints: Ask whether each rule reflects something users feel.
Check the duration window on error and CPU alerts.
Look for a missing latency or availability objective.
Revise the rules: CPU pages are noisy, every 5xx pages, and latency has no alert.

artifact.title: alerts.yaml
artifact.caption: The current production alert rules.
artifact.content:
groups:
  - name: campus
    rules:
      - alert: HighCpu
        expr: cpu_percent > 40
        for: 1m
        severity: page
      - alert: AnyServerError
        expr: increase(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[1m]) > 0
        for: 0m
        severity: page
      - alert: DiskAlmostFull
        expr: disk_free_percent < 5
        severity: ticket

findings.label: CPU above forty percent pages after one minute even when requests are healthy.
There is no latency or availability objective for the checkout path.
Disk pressure is only a ticket even at five percent free.
Adding a rule for every known cause improves the on-call signal.

verdicts.label: Revise around user-facing SLOs and error-budget burn

steps.explanation: CPU is a cause, not a symptom. Page on sustained user-visible error and latency, and keep disk pressure actionable before it becomes an outage.

steps.title: Make paging meaningful
hints: A page should correspond to something users feel.
Labels with unbounded values multiply series.
Select symptoms, SLO burn, bounded labels, and actionable pages; reject more alerts as better.

statements.label: Page on sustained user-visible errors or latency, not on a single cause metric.
Error-budget burn rate connects alerting to the reliability target.
Metric labels should stay bounded; user id is usually a bad label.
Every page should have an action the responder can take.
More alerts always produce better reliability.

steps.explanation: Good alerting is selective, symptom-based, and actionable. More rules can reduce signal by exhausting the responder.
